title: The road to Damascus (Acts 9:1–9)
hookLine: Saul, hunting Christians, is blinded by light and hears: why persecute me?

cards: Saul is breathing out threats and slaughter, Acts says, against the followers of Jesus, who at this point call their movement the Way.
He's the young man who held the coats while Stephen died, and he's no bystander anymore.
He asks the high priest for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, a week's journey north, so that any followers he finds there, men or women, can be brought back to Jerusalem in chains.
He's certain, organized, on the road with his papers and companions. Just outside Damascus, at midday, a light from heaven flashes around him, and he falls to the ground.

teach.b: Lying in the dust, he hears a voice. In the King James Bible: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" He asks, "Who art thou, Lord?"
And the answer: "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest." Listen to that word me. Saul has never met Jesus; he's been hunting Jesus's followers.
Christians have heard in that line, for two thousand years, that what's done to his people is done to him. Saul gets up, opens his eyes, and sees nothing.
The men with him lead him by the hand into the city, and for three days he's blind, and doesn't eat or drink. The man who came to drag people out in chains is led in by the hand.
Today's word, conversion, comes from the Latin for turning around, and the Greek word Acts uses elsewhere means the same: a turning. Two common mistakes.
There's no horse: well-known paintings put him on one, but the text only says he fell to the ground. And God doesn't rename him Paul here.
Later, Acts says Saul, who also is called Paul: a Hebrew name and a Roman one, side by side.
Paul himself, in his letters, describes this moment less as leaving his people's faith and more as a calling, the way God called the prophets. Scholars still discuss how best to describe it.

Luke thought it mattered so much that Acts tells it three times, and many churches keep a feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul on January twenty-fifth. The hunter becomes the one who carries the news.

how: Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches, among others, keep the Feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul on January 25. Many Christians speak of their own conversion as a turning, whether sudden like Paul's or slow over years.

o: moving your membership to a new church
a sudden vision that proves a faith is true
a turning around, a life changing direction

games.q: you're Saul, face down in the dust, blinded, and a voice asks why you're persecuting him. what do you say?
o: nothing. you get up and carry on to Damascus.
games.why: he asks, who art thou, Lord? the answer is: I am Jesus whom thou persecutest. then he's led into the city by the hand.

practice: Saul only heard the voice because he was stopped. So stop, and listen to what's around you: traffic, a fridge, birds, your own breathing.
Then listen inside for something you've been sure about, charging down the road with, that might need a second look. Don't argue with it. If you pray, you can ask, as Saul did, who are you, Lord?

wordCard.voice: Conversion. A turning around. Saul on the road to Damascus, stopped in the dust and led by the hand.

orig.note: Greek: a turning around. Acts 15:3 uses it, and the KJV renders it conversion.
